title: Substring XOR Queries
statement:
You get a binary string `s` and a list `queries` where `queries[i] = [first_i, second_i]`. For each query, look for a non-empty contiguous substring of `s` whose value, read as a binary number (leading zeros allowed and ignored), is a number `val` with `val XOR first_i == second_i`.

- Among all such substrings, take the shortest; if several are equally short, take the one that starts earliest.
- The query's answer is that substring's 0-indexed start and end positions `[left_i, right_i]`, or `[-1, -1]` if no substring works.

Return the list of answers, one per query, in the order of `queries`.
notes:
## Intuition

Since `val XOR first == second` is the same as `val == first XOR second`, each query asks for one exact number. Checking every substring per query is far too slow, but the numbers are small: `first` and `second` are below 2^30, so the wanted value fits in 30 bits. A shortest substring with a positive value starts with a `1` (a leading zero only makes it longer), so it has at most 30 characters. That leaves at most 30 · n candidate substrings, which we can index once in a hash map.

## Approach

1. Walk `left` from 0 to the end of `s`.
2. If `s[left]` is `0`, the substring `"0"` is the shortest way to make the value 0; record `[left, left]` for 0 if nothing is stored yet, and move on.
3. Otherwise extend `right` up to 30 characters, building `value` bit by bit, and store `[left, right]` for each value not seen before. Because `left` only grows, the first record of a value is the earliest start; and all `1`-led substrings of one value have the same length, so it is also the shortest.
4. For each query, look up `first ^ second` in `firstSeen`, defaulting to `[-1, -1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "101101"`. From `left = 0` we store 1 → `[0,0]`, 2 → `[0,1]`, 5 → `[0,2]`, 11, 22, 45. `left = 1` is a zero: 0 → `[1,1]`. From `left = 2` we store 3 → `[2,3]` and more. The queries want `0 ^ 5 = 5` → `[0,2]` and `1 ^ 2 = 3` → `[2,3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(30 · n + q): at most 30 extensions per start, then one lookup per query.
- Space: O(30 · n) for the map in the worst case.

## Pitfalls

- Do not extend from a `0`: `"01"` would claim value 1 before a later, shorter `"1"`.
- Value 0 needs its own case; a `1`-led substring never produces it.
- Stop at 30 bits; longer substrings cannot match and their values overflow 32-bit integers.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `firstSeen` | value → `[left, right]` of its shortest, earliest substring |
| `left`, `right` | start and end of the current substring |
| `value` | the substring `s[left..right]` as a number |
| `target` | `first ^ second`, the value a query needs |
| `answer` | the result for each query |

narration.2: firstSeen maps each value to the shortest, earliest substring that produces it.
narration.4: Try every start position from left to right, so the first record of a value has the smallest start.
narration.5: A substring starting with 0 is never the shortest way to write a positive value.
narration.6: But "0" itself is the shortest substring with value 0; keep its first position.
narration.7: Skip the longer substrings that start with this zero.
narration.9: value holds the number spelled by s[left..right].
narration.10: Extend the substring one bit at a time, but never past 30 bits.
narration.11: Shift the value left and add the new bit.
narration.12: Store this value only if no earlier start produced it.
narration.18: val ^ first == second exactly when val == first ^ second.
narration.19: Look up the stored substring, or report [-1, -1] if none produces the value.
narration.21: Return all answers in query order.
